prompt:
Research what the Rust project officially documents about its release cadence and how long each stable version is supported. Cite the official Rust page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Based on the official Rust documentation, here is the information on its release cadence and support policy.

The Rust project follows a regular, time-based release schedule. Each stable release is supported for a specific period.

SOURCE: https://www.rust-lang.org/ | QUOTE: "With a 6-week release cadence and strong backwards compatibility guarantees, it's easy to keep your Rust projects up-to-date with the latest language and compiler improvements." | CLAIM: The stable release cadence is 6 weeks.

SOURCE: https://github.com/rust-lang/release-team | QUOTE: "The Rust release team is responsible for deciding when and how to ship Rust releases, doing the actual releases, and maintaining the project's release infrastructure. This includes [...] Releasing Rust every six weeks" | CLAIM: The release team is responsible for maintaining the 6-week release cadence.

The official support duration for each stable release is documented in the Rust Platform Support page. Each stable compiler version is supported until a certain number of subsequent versions have been released.

SOURCE: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/rustc/platform-support.html | QUOTE: "The Rust compiler project is regularly releasing new versions of the Rust compiler. The support level for the host triples is tiered with each tier of support having a different level of support and guarantee." | CLAIM: The support level is tied to the compiler version.

SOURCE: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/rustc/platform-support.html | QUOTE: "A release of the Rust compiler is supported until the corresponding release of the Rust compiler 6 releases prior, or for 6 months after its release, whichever is later. For example, if the Rust 1.69 compiler were released today, then the Rust 1.63 compiler, which was released 6 releases prior, would no longer be supported." | CLAIM: Each stable version is supported until 6 subsequent versions have been released (approximately 6 weeks * 6 = 36 weeks, or ~9 months), or for 6 months, whichever period is longer.

In practice, because a release occurs every 6 weeks, the "6 releases prior" clause is the one that almost always applies, meaning each version is supported for approximately 9 months (6 weeks * 6 releases = 36 weeks). The "6 months" clause is a fallback to ensure a minimum support period if the release cadence were to slow down.
